title: Why the other queue always moves faster
description: It does not. You only notice the times it does, because losing to the other lane hurts more than winning feels good.

title: Why ten thousand steps
description: The number came from a Japanese pedometer marketing campaign in 1965. It is still the number, because round numbers become goals whether they deserve to or not.

title: Why you keep watching a bad movie
description: Forty minutes in, you know it is terrible. You stay anyway, because leaving would waste the forty minutes. It would not. They are already gone.

title: Why you tip more when the screen asks
description: The card machine turns to face you with three buttons and a queue behind you. Twenty percent suddenly seems reasonable. Nothing about the coffee changed.

title: Why the medium popcorn always wins
description: Small $5, medium $8, large $8.50. Nobody buys the medium. That is exactly the point of the medium.

title: Why the second slice never tastes as good
description: The first bite of anything is the best one you will get. Economists have a dull name for this and a surprisingly useful lesson inside it.

title: The lost ticket
description: You lose a $50 ticket on the way to the theatre. Do you buy another? Now imagine you lose $50 cash instead. Most people answer the two questions differently.

title: The gym membership you never use
description: You are not lazy. You were sold a version of yourself that does not exist yet, and the pricing was designed around the gap.

title: Why waiting rooms feel longer than they are
description: Ten minutes not knowing feels like twenty. Ten minutes with a number and a screen feels like five. The clinic can change the second without touching the first.

title: Why you cannot pick anything to watch
description: Thousands of options, thirty minutes of scrolling, and you watch the thing you have already seen. Too much choice does not free you. It stalls you.

title: Why your doctor cannot tell you what to do
description: Two treatments, same survival odds, different side effects. There is no medical answer to which is better, and that is not a failure of medicine.

title: Why a bigger plate makes you eat more
description: The same portion looks small on a large plate and generous on a small one. Your eyes decide how full you are before your stomach gets a say.

title: Why free shipping costs you money
description: You added a $14 item you did not want to avoid a $6 delivery fee. Everyone does it. Here is the switch in your head that got flipped.

title: Only three left in stock
description: There were four this morning. There will be four tomorrow. Scarcity is the oldest trick in the shop, and it still works on you.

title: Why a pay rise stops feeling like one
description: It took about eight weeks for your last raise to become invisible. That is not ingratitude. It is how reference points work, and you can use it.

title: The question behind the question
description: Survey answers are not read off a preference sitting in your head. They are constructed on the spot, and the way you ask changes what gets built.

title: The Power of Free
description: Why 'free' is not just a low price. It changes how we decide, sometimes against our own interest.

title: The Tyranny of the Default
description: The option you never chose is often the one you end up with. Defaults quietly shape huge decisions.

title: Why Your Apps Autoplay the Next Episode
description: The attention economy is built on removing tiny frictions and adding them where it wants you to stay.

title: The benchmark before bias
description: Why behavioural economics starts with rational choice rather than replacing it.

title: Why 19,998 Feels Cheaper Than 20,000
description: A tiny change in a number can produce a large change in how it feels. Blame the left-most digit.

title: What I got wrong about vaccine mandates
description: I assumed opposition ran along a single line from pro to anti. The data said otherwise, and the design implications were not what I expected.

title: What a discrete choice experiment actually measures
description: A plain guide to what a DCE can tell you, and what it cannot.

title: Why People Buy Both Insurance and Lottery Tickets
description: The same person often buys insurance and a lottery ticket. Probability weighting explains how both can be attractive at once.

title: Averages hide the people who matter
description: Why preference heterogeneity, not the average, is often the real finding.

title: Loss Aversion in Health, Pricing, and Public Policy
description: Losses tend to loom larger than equivalent gains. That simple asymmetry reshapes how people value treatments, prices, and policies.

title: What eye tracking reveals about how we choose
description: Using eye tracking to see how people read a choice task, and why it matters.

title: Risk versus Ambiguity: Why Unknown Probabilities Change Decisions
description: Risk is when the odds are known. Ambiguity is when they are not. People treat the two very differently, and it matters for new health technologies.

title: Does feedback help people make better choices?
description: Giving respondents feedback in a preference task can guide them, or mislead them.

title: The Allais Paradox and What It Reveals about Rational Choice
description: A famous pair of choices that most people get 'wrong' by the standard model. The Allais paradox shows why the independence axiom is hard to keep.

title: What preference research adds to the vaccine mandate debate
description: Mandates are usually argued in absolutes. Preference research shows the trade-offs.

title: The Ellsberg Paradox, Ambiguity Aversion, and New Health Technologies
description: People prefer a bet with known odds to an equivalent bet with unknown odds. The Ellsberg paradox shows why, and why it matters for new technologies.

title: The fifty dollar question
description: A small experiment you can run on yourself in under a minute, and what it reveals about how you actually value your own time.

title: Why I build decision tools
description: Turning preference studies into tools that decision-makers can actually use.

title: Why 99% does not feel like 100%
description: The certainty effect: why eliminating the last sliver of risk is worth more than removing an equivalent sliver in the middle, and what that does to health decisions.
